what_its_for: Silodosin is used to treat the symptoms of an enlarged prostate (also called benign prostatic hyperplasia or BPH) in adult men. It helps relax the muscles in your prostate and bladder neck, making it easier to urinate. Common symptoms it helps with include a weak urine stream, needing to urinate often or urgently, and trouble starting to urinate.
how_to_take: Take silodosin by mouth, once a day, with a meal. Swallow the capsule whole — do not crush, chew, or open it. Taking it with food helps your body absorb it properly and may reduce the chance of dizziness. Try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember.
dosing: The usual dose is 8 mg (one capsule) taken once daily with a meal. If you have kidney problems, your doctor may lower your dose to 4 mg once daily. Always take exactly the dose your doctor prescribed. Do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose the following day with a meal. Do not take two doses in one day to make up for a missed one. Taking a double dose can increase your risk of side effects, especially dizziness.
storage: Store silodosin at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it in a dry place, away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. If you no longer need this medication, ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking silodosin, as it can increase dizziness and the risk of falling. Be careful when standing up quickly from a sitting or lying position, especially in the first few days of treatment, as silodosin can cause a sudden drop in blood pressure (called orthostatic hypotension) that may make you feel lightheaded or faint. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you. Tell your eye doctor (ophthalmologist) that you take silodosin before any eye surgery, as it can cause a condition called Intraoperative Floppy Iris Syndrome (IFIS) during cataract surgery. Avoid taking other alpha-blocker medicines (such as tamsulosin or doxazosin) at the same time unless your doctor says it is okay.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get medical help right away if you experience: a painful erection that lasts more than 4 hours (priapism) — this is a medical emergency; severe dizziness or fainting; signs of a serious allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of your face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing; very low blood pressure symptoms like feeling faint when you stand up. Also contact your doctor if your urinary symptoms get worse or do not improve after a few weeks of treatment.
when_it_works: Some men notice an improvement in their urinary symptoms within a few days of starting silodosin, but it may take 2 to 4 weeks to feel the full benefit. Keep taking it as prescribed even if you feel well. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Silodosin is only approved for use in adult men. Women and children should not take this medicine. If you have severe kidney disease or severe liver disease, you should not take silodosin. If you have moderate kidney problems, your doctor will lower your dose. Always tell your doctor about all your health conditions and all the medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting silodosin.
